teile.text: Who really owned Coca-Cola in 1888? Three versions of the drink were on sale that year, from three separate businesses.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: a blue-eyed presenter in fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch stands on a gaslit 1880s Atlanta street, three drugstore fronts behind him, warm dusk light, medium shot.

teile.text: This video answers one question. How did Asa Candler take control, and what did one cheap decision cost later?
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the fedora-wearing presenter in grey suit checks his gold pocket watch beside a horse-drawn carriage on a busy 1880s Atlanta street, amber light, wide shot, calm sky above.

teile.text: Be sure to like, share and save this video. Now, back to Atlanta.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter steps through the doorway of a Victorian drugstore with glass jars and wooden shelves, warm lantern glow, medium shot from the street, no readable signage.

teile.name: A tonic and a ban
teile.text: John Pemberton was a Confederate colonel, wounded in the Civil War. He became addicted to morphine and sought a substitute.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous wounded 1860s officer in a worn grey coat sits by a window in a quiet room, hand pressed to his side, soft morning light, medium shot, illustrative figure only.

teile.text: At his drugstore in Columbus, Georgia, he registered a nerve tonic in 1885. It was called Pemberton's French Wine Coca, and it included kola nut, a source of caffeine.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous 1880s druggist in an apron pours dark liquid from a glass flask into a bottle behind a wooden counter, shelves of unlabeled jars, warm lamplight, medium shot.

teile.text: Then a legal obstacle appeared. Atlanta and Fulton County passed prohibition legislation in 1886. Pemberton responded by developing Coca-Cola, a non-alcoholic version of his tonic.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: anonymous 1880s townspeople gather on a courthouse-lined Atlanta street, a man hammers a wooden barrel shut as others watch, overcast daylight, wide shot, no writing visible.

teile.text: He marketed it as the temperance drink. That appealed to many people, because the temperance movement enjoyed wide support.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: anonymous men and women in 1880s dress listen to a speaker on a small outdoor platform, ribbons on lapels, sunlit street, medium-wide shot, no signs or text.

teile.text: The first sales came at Jacob's Pharmacy in Atlanta on May 8, 1886. A glass cost five cents. Pemberton ran the first advertisement three weeks later in the Atlanta Journal.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous soda jerk in 1880s apron slides a glass of dark fizzing drink across a marble drugstore counter to a customer's waiting hand, warm light, close medium shot.

teile.text: Pemberton also sold it as a patent medicine. He claimed it cured many diseases, including morphine addiction, indigestion, nerve disorders and headaches.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous Victorian customer holds her temple while a druggist hands over a small brown bottle across a wooden counter, apothecary shelves, soft window light, medium shot.

teile.text: The name came from two original ingredients: coca leaves and kola nuts. Soon, though, the name itself would become the fight.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: close shot of a wooden tray holding green coca leaves on one side and brown kola nuts on the other, a hand sorting them, warm side light, shallow depth.

teile.name: Three owners, one name
teile.text: By January 1888, Pemberton had formed a co-partnership with four Atlanta businessmen. Yet ownership was still unclear.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: five anonymous men in 1880s suits and bowler hats stand around a wooden table in a dim office, one older man among them, serious faces, lamplight, medium-wide shot.

teile.text: Years later, Candler himself said under testimony that he had a stake in Pemberton's company as early as 1887. No signed document records it.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous older man in a dark suit sits in a wooden witness chair, hand raised, attentive listeners in the background, soft courtroom light, medium shot, no text.

teile.text: John Pemberton declared that the name Coca-Cola belonged to his son, Charley. The other two manufacturers could keep using the formula.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous older man in a waistcoat rests a hand on the shoulder of a younger man in a drugstore back room, illustrative figures, warm dusk light, medium shot.

teile.text: That mattered. Charley became a major shareholder in the March 1888 incorporation filing, made in his father's place.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous young man in 1880s coat sits at a large oak table among older businessmen, pen in hand, faces turned toward him, tense lamplit room, medium shot.

teile.text: His control of the name became a continual thorn in Asa Candler's side. So how did Candler move in?
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the fedora-wearing presenter in grey suit and dark tie stands at a drugstore window, gold watch chain visible, looking toward a rival shop across the street, golden afternoon light, medium shot.

teile.text: On April 14, his firm made a deal with Charley, with John cosigning. For $50 down and $500 in 30 days, it got Charley's one-third interest. But Charley kept the name.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: two anonymous 1880s men shake hands over a desk while a third man stands behind as witness, a few coins on the wood, warm lamplight, medium shot, no papers shown.

teile.text: Candler's son later wrote, in a 1950 biography, that Asa bought a third of the formula. The deal was actually with Charley.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous elderly man in a 1950 suit sits at a study desk by a window, pen resting, gazing outward thoughtfully, soft afternoon light, medium shot.

teile.text: Three days later, Candler paid another $750 for half of the Walker and Dozier interest shares.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora counts out bills into an anonymous partner's open hand across a drugstore counter, gold pocket watch glinting, warm light, close medium shot.

teile.text: Owning pieces still wasn't winning. Candler sold his own recipe as Yum Yum and Koke, while Charley sold a cruder mixture as Coca-Cola.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: two rival 1880s drugstore soda counters side by side on one street, different anonymous clerks serving customers, split by a brick pillar, bright daylight, wide shot, no readable signs.

teile.text: Neither of Candler's names caught on. By the middle of 1888, he was anxious to establish a firmer legal claim.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in fedora and grey suit stands alone in a quiet drugstore with unsold bottles on the counter, rubbing his chin, late afternoon light, medium shot.

teile.name: The race for the name
teile.text: Then, on August 16, John Pemberton died of stomach cancer. Candler decided to move swiftly toward full control.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: anonymous mourners in black 1880s clothing gather under bare trees at a cemetery, a lone man in grey suit and fedora watches from the edge, overcast light, wide shot.

teile.text: Charley unnerved Candler more than anyone. Candler is said to have moved quickly to buy the rights to the name. One of several stories says he offered Charley's mother $300 in cash at the funeral.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous woman in a black veil stands among mourners as a man in a grey suit speaks quietly to her, hat in hand, muted graveside light, medium shot, clearly a retold story.

teile.text: His son's book says that on August 30, Asa became sole proprietor, a fact stated on letterheads, invoices and advertising.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the fedora presenter in grey suit stands at a printing shop, anonymous workers feeding sheets into a press behind him, ink-stained hands, warm industrial light, medium-wide shot.

teile.text: To make that true, he negotiated with Margaret Dozier and her brother Woolfolk Walker. They agreed on $1,000, payable through a series of notes.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous woman and her brother in 1880s dress sit across a table from the presenter in grey suit and fedora, calm negotiation, window light, medium shot.

teile.text: By May 1, 1889, Candler was claiming full ownership. His total investment over the years came to $2,300.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora leans back in his office chair, satisfied, gold pocket watch in hand, warm lamp glow, shelves of bottles behind, medium shot.

teile.text: So who owned Coca-Cola by then? Candler claimed it. But the paper trail has problems, and the doubts began with signatures.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in fedora and grey suit stands at a dim office window with a thoughtful frown, a half-open drawer beside him, cool evening light, medium shot, no papers visible.

teile.text: In 1914, Margaret Dozier said her signature on the 1888 bill of sale had been forged.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous older woman in 1914 dress stands firmly in a plain office, one hand raised in protest, men in suits listening, cool daylight, medium shot, no papers shown.

teile.text: Later analysis of similar documents suggested John Pemberton's signature was most likely forged too. Some accounts say Charley prompted it.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous examiner with a magnifying glass leans over a desk under a bright lamp, face intent, shadows around, tight medium shot, document face-down and out of frame.

teile.text: In 1910, Candler had the earliest records of the Coca-Cola Company destroyed. The action was claimed to be part of a move to new offices.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: anonymous workers in 1910 clothing carry wooden crates through an office hallway while a furnace glows in a side room, dusty light, wide shot.

teile.name: The one-dollar contract
teile.text: Candler's marketing tactics, the source says, led Coca-Cola to dominate the global soft-drink market. But one decision about bottles caused trouble for decades.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora looks out an office window at a wagon of glass bottles being unloaded below, thoughtful, golden light, medium shot.

teile.text: Two Chattanooga entrepreneurs, Benjamin Thomas and Joseph Whitehead, proposed bottling the drink. They were so persuasive that Candler signed a contract giving them control of the procedure.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: two anonymous eager men in 1890s suits lean toward the seated presenter in grey suit and fedora across a desk, gesturing, he reaches for a pen, lamplit office, medium shot.

teile.text: The price was one dollar, and Candler never collected it. He later realized he had made a grave mistake. He remained very content just selling his company's syrup.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora stands at a counter of syrup jugs, an empty open palm in front of him, regretful expression, warm shop light, medium shot.

teile.text: In 1899, Chattanooga became the site of the first Coca-Cola bottling company.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: anonymous workers roll wooden syrup barrels onto a railway platform in a Tennessee town, smoke from a distant locomotive, hazy daylight, wide shot.

teile.text: The contract was loosely termed. It set bottles at five cents each and had no fixed duration. That led to a fixed price of Coca-Cola from 1886 to 1959.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora rubs his forehead at his desk, a row of glass bottles lined up in front of him, shadowed lamplight, close medium shot.

teile.text: The bottlers also subcontracted to other companies, effectively becoming parent bottlers. The loose contract stayed problematic for the company for decades.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: a mid-century shopkeeper hands an ice-cold glass bottle to a customer across a store counter, rows of bottles behind, warm retro light, medium shot, no labels visible.

teile.text: On September 12, 1919, investors led by Ernest Woodruff's Trust Company bought the company for $25 million. They offered 500,000 shares to the public at $40 a share.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: anonymous 1910s executives in three-piece suits gather around a long boardroom table, shafts of light through tall windows, medium-wide shot, no text.

teile.text: Ernest's son Robert Woodruff became president in 1923. The company began distributing bottles as six-packs, encouraging customers to buy the drink for their home.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous 1920s family at a kitchen table, a father setting a carton of six glass bottles down, children reaching eagerly, warm window light, medium shot, no labels.

teile.text: For decades, the company preferred its full name. It feared coke would become a generic trademark, and it didn't want to be confused with a coal byproduct.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: 1930s delivery men carry wooden crates of glass bottles from a truck into a corner store, cheerful street, late afternoon light, wide shot, no readable text.

teile.text: It officially adopted Coke in 1941 and registered it in 1945.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: a 1940s shopkeeper in a paper cap serves two customers at a soda counter, glass bottles in a cooler behind him, warm retro light, medium shot, no readable text.

teile.text: The formula, meanwhile, remains a trade secret. Only a handful of anonymous employees know it, and the company uses that secrecy as a marketing aid.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora stands beside a heavy steel vault door in a dim corridor, one finger raised to his lips, dramatic side light, medium shot.

teile.text: Today the company produces concentrate and sells it to licensed bottlers worldwide. Those bottlers hold exclusive territory contracts.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: workers in modern caps watch glass bottles move along a bright bottling line, dark liquid filling each one, clean industrial light, medium-wide shot, no labels.

teile.text: Coke products were sold in over 200 countries and territories in 2013. Consumers drank more than 1.8 billion company servings each day.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: busy international harbor at dawn with cargo containers and cranes, trucks loading crates of red-capped bottles, wide cinematic shot, warm glow, no text.

teile.name: The answer
teile.text: So who owned Coca-Cola in 1888? No single person. Charley held the name, others held shares, and three businesses sold the drink.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch stands before a row of Victorian shop windows, hand on watch chain, golden evening light, medium shot.

teile.text: Candler fixed that step by step. He bought shares, settled with Walker and Dozier, and claimed full ownership by May 1889.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora shakes hands with an anonymous man across a drugstore counter while another watches, warm lamplight, medium-wide shot, no papers shown.

teile.text: He did it on a total investment of $2,300. Yet the record stays disputed, from the forgery claim to the destroyed records.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora stands at a dim office desk beside an open empty strongbox and a pile of loose crates, serious expression, side lamplight, medium shot.

teile.text: His other deal looked tiny at the time. A one-dollar contract he never collected tied bottlers to a five-cent price with no end date.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: two anonymous 1890s bottlers in vests and the presenter in grey suit and fedora shake hands in a lamplit office, a crate of empty bottles on the floor, medium shot.

teile.text: The source links that contract to a fixed price lasting until 1959 and to legal problems for decades.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora watches a long line of glass bottles roll past in a factory, expression serious, warm industrial light, medium-wide shot.

teile.text: Compare the two deals. He spent $2,300 in total to claim the drink. He never collected one dollar for the bottling contract.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in grey suit and fedora stands between a drugstore door and a bottling shed door on an Atlanta street, looking from one to the other, golden light, wide shot.

teile.text: The bottling deal had no end date, and its legal problems outlasted the fight over the name by decades.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: anonymous lawyers in mid-century suits argue around a long table in a smoky office, one man gesturing sharply, the presenter watching from the doorway, dim light, medium-wide shot, no papers visible.

teile.text: That's the answer: ownership of Coca-Cola began as a tangle of names, shares and signatures. Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the fedora-wearing presenter in grey suit walks away down an Atlanta street at sunset, a single glass bottle in hand, long warm shadows, wide shot, calm sky above.

entwurf.beschreibung: Asa Candler claimed full ownership of Coca-Cola by May 1889, though parts of the paper trail are disputed. His one-dollar bottling contract then caused legal problems for decades.
